extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of American colonial history
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter-level historical analysis of the social, political, and legal origins of Anglo-American (especially New England and Virginia) colonies in the 17th century, explaining institutional causes and consequences. Focuses on settlers' composition, modes of colonization, early laws, and the roots of American local democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Land as the basis of an aristocracy
rubrics_metrics.description: "Land is the basis of an aristocracy, which clings to the soil that supports it; for it is not by privileges alone, nor by birth, but by landed property handed down from generation to generation, that an aristocracy is constituted."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that territorial (inherited) landed property — not merely wealth, privileges, or birth — is the structural foundation of an aristocracy; absence of territorial fortunes yields no aristocracy but merely classes of rich and poor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes leading to colonial democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Emigrants "had in general no notion of superiority over one another"; poverty and misfortune produce equality; land tended to be broken into small portions cultivated by proprietors themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues two main causes produced democratic elements: (1) emigrants' lack of ingrained superiority and (2) economic conditions (small owner-cultivated holdings making territorial aristocracy unviable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of slavery on southern society
rubrics_metrics.description: Slavery "dishonors labor; it introduces idleness into society, and, with idleness, ignorance and pride, luxury and distress. It enervates the powers of the mind, and benumbs the activity of man."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attributes the distinctive character, manners, and laws of the southern states largely to the early introduction of slavery (noting its origin c.1620 in Virginia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlers' composition and colony character (New England vs. others)
rubrics_metrics.description: New England settlers "belonged to the more independent classes"; "All, without a single exception, had received a good education" and many were known in Europe for talents and acquirements; their emigration was "purely intellectual" rather than for wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Links the social origins (middle-class, educated, family migrants, religious motives) of New England colonists to the formation of different social, moral, and political institutions than colonies founded by adventurers or convicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Puritanism as political doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Puritanism was "not merely a religious doctrine, but it corresponded in many points with the most absolute democratic and republican theories."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positions Puritan religious beliefs as closely tied to democratic/republican political practices; persecution at home drove politically-minded groups to found self-governing colonies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early social contract / covenantal self-government (Mayflower Compact)
rubrics_metrics.description: The settlers "covenant and combine ourselves together into a civil body politic ... and by virtue hereof do enact, constitute, and frame, such just and equal laws, ordinances, acts, constitutions, and officers ... as shall be thought most meet and convenient for the general good of the colony" (1620 act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses the Compact as evidence that colonists intentionally formed self-governing political societies under a covenant model, establishing laws and officers by mutual consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of colonization and impact on liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Three systems: (1) crown-appointed governors ruling in the king's name; (2) grants to individuals/companies who sold lands and governed; (3) allowing a number of emigrants to constitute a political society and govern themselves (the last "remarkably favorable to liberty").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies the third mode (settler self-government) as adopted in New England and as a principal cause of greater civil freedom in British colonies compared to other empires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mosaic-derived penal code in Connecticut (1650)
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislators of Connecticut "borrow their provisions from the text of holy writ": the preamble says, 'Whoever shall worship any other God than the Lord ... shall surely be put to death.' Blasphemy, sorcery, adultery, and rape were punished with death; even a son offending parents could receive the same penalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes direct borrowing from Exodus, Leviticus, and Deuteronomy; notes that statutes prescribed capital punishment frequently on paper even if enforcement was rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative intervention into conscience and morals
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislature "constantly invaded the domain of conscience" regulating adultery, rape, intercourse between unmarried persons (punishments including pecuniary penalty, whipping, or marriage), compulsory attendance at divine service, and severe penalties (even death) for differing rites or dissenters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates the theocratic or moral-regulatory nature of early New England laws with examples (punishments for 'improper language', prohibition of tobacco, banishment and whipping of Quakers and Baptists, death penalty threat for returning Catholic priests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles of modern constitutions recognized
rubrics_metrics.description: The general principles which are the groundwork of modern constitutions — "the intervention of the people in public affairs, the free voting of taxes, the responsibility of authorities, personal liberty, and trial by jury" — were all positively established in New England laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that New England law anticipated key constitutional principles that were imperfect or absent in contemporary Europe, and that these had practical applications and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Township independence as nucleus of American liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: In New England, 'the township was organized before the county, the county before the state, the state before the Union.' Towns named their own magistrates, rated themselves, and levied their own taxes; affairs were discussed 'as at Athens, in the market-place, by a general assembly of the citizens.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames local self-government (township autonomy, direct assemblies) as the political structure that enabled broad democratic participation and became the 'life and mainspring' of American liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral and militia provisions in Connecticut
rubrics_metrics.description: In Connecticut the electoral body 'consisted, from its origin, of the whole number of citizens'; 'all the executive functionaries were elected, including the governor.' Citizens above sixteen 'were obliged to bear arms' and formed a militia that appointed its own officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies inclusive electoral franchise and locally controlled militia as institutional arrangements fostering civic responsibility and readiness to defend the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early public-welfare and administrative provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws provided for the condition of the poor, maintenance of roads (surveyors appointed), registers in every parish for public deliberations and vital records, clerks to keep registers, officers to administer vacant inheritances and arbitrate land disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlights that New England legislation included many practical administrative measures for social needs and public order that were more comprehensive than contemporaneous practices in France.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of puritanical/fantastical civic regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws forbade the use of tobacco; associations formed to check 'worldly luxury' such as long hair; innkeepers were forbidden to furnish more than a certain quantity of liquor to each customer; simple lying 'whenever it may be injurious' was punished by fine or flogging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses these particulars to show the zeal and sometimes petty character of moral legislation — severe, detailed, and often voted freely by the community itself.
